blocks.text: Pretraining and fine-tuning are both training processes applied to the same kind of model, but they differ enormously in scale, in objective, and in who typically performs them.

Understanding that difference clearly is important before going deeper into fine-tuning methods, because fine-tuning only works because pretraining already did the hard, expensive work of teaching the model language, reasoning, and general knowledge.
1. Two Different Training Phases
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448215003-656994808.png

Every large language model in production today has gone through pretraining first, an enormous, general training run, and typically one or more fine-tuning stages afterward, smaller and more targeted training runs on top of that foundation.

These two phases use the same underlying mechanism, weights adjusted through gradient descent to reduce a loss value, but they differ in essentially every other dimension, data, scale, objective, and cost.
2. What Pretraining Actually Optimizes For
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448215003-341583420.png

Pretraining starts from randomly initialized weights and trains the model on a simple, broad objective, usually predicting the next token in a huge and varied stream of text, code, and sometimes other data types.

There is no single narrow task being optimized during pretraining, the goal is general competence, grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and coding ability, absorbed indirectly from the sheer scale and variety of the data.
3. The Scale of Pretraining Data and Compute

blocks.alt: The Scale of Pretraining Data and Compute
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448215003-220044348.png

Modern pretraining runs consume trillions of tokens of text, run across clusters of thousands of specialized GPUs, and take weeks or months to complete, at a cost that can reach tens of millions of dollars for the largest models.

This scale is precisely why pretraining is performed by a small number of well resourced labs and companies, while fine-tuning, by contrast, is accessible to individual teams and even individual developers.

blocks.text: 4. What Fine-Tuning Optimizes For
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448215004-614750975.png

Fine-tuning starts from the already pretrained weights and continues training, but now the data is deliberately narrow, examples that show exactly the task, tone, or format you want the model to specialize in.

The objective during fine-tuning is often still next token prediction under the hood, but applied to a dataset chosen specifically to push the model toward one kind of behavior, rather than general competence across everything.
5. The Scale of Fine-Tuning Data and Compute

blocks.alt: The Scale of Fine-Tuning Data and Compute
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448215004-138431135.png

A fine-tuning run typically uses somewhere between a few hundred and a few million examples, runs on a single GPU or a small handful of them, and finishes in hours to a couple of days rather than weeks or months.

blocks.title: Orders of magnitude, not a small difference
blocks.content: The gap between pretraining and fine-tuning scale is not incremental, it commonly spans four to six orders of magnitude in both data volume and compute cost.

blocks.text: 6. Objective Functions, Broad Prediction vs Narrow Alignment

blocks.alt: Objective Functions, Broad Prediction vs Narrow Alignment
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448215005-737447025.png
During pretraining, the model is being pushed to correctly predict text drawn from an enormous variety of sources and topics, an objective that is broad almost by definition.

During fine-tuning, the model is being pushed to match a much narrower distribution, the specific examples in the fine-tuning dataset, which is why fine-tuning can shift behavior noticeably even though it changes the underlying weights by a comparatively small amount.
7. Who Performs Each Stage
Pretraining is almost always performed by the organization that releases the base model, given the scale of compute and data required, and most fine-tuning consumers never touch this stage directly.

Fine-tuning, by contrast, is regularly performed by individual companies, teams, and even solo developers, since it requires only a fraction of the resources and can be run on modest hardware for smaller models or efficient methods.

code.content:
# Pretraining, conceptually, run by a small number of labs
model = train_from_scratch(
    data=trillions_of_tokens,
    compute=thousands_of_gpus,
    duration_weeks=8
)

# Fine-tuning, run by a much wider range of teams
fine_tuned = fine_tune(
    base_model=pretrained_checkpoint,
    data=task_specific_examples,
    compute=one_or_a_few_gpus,
    duration_hours=6
)

blocks.text: 8. Pretraining Sets the Ceiling, Fine-Tuning Sets the Direction

blocks.alt: Pretraining Sets the Ceiling, Fine-Tuning Sets the Direction
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448215005-916465575.png

A useful mental model is that pretraining determines the ceiling of what a model can possibly do, its raw reasoning ability, its language fluency, its general knowledge, while fine-tuning determines the direction that capability gets pointed in for a specific job.

No amount of fine-tuning can give a small, weakly pretrained model reasoning ability it never had, and no amount of pretraining alone reliably produces the narrow, consistent behavior that fine-tuning is good at supplying.
9. A Side by Side Comparison

Putting the two phases next to each other makes the relationship clearer, pretraining builds the broad foundation once, at enormous cost, and fine-tuning reshapes a copy of that foundation repeatedly, cheaply, for many different downstream tasks.

blocks.text: Worked Example

A lab spends two months and several million dollars pretraining a seven billion parameter model on a broad mixture of web text, books, and code, producing a model that can hold a reasonable conversation about almost any general topic.

A separate company downloads that pretrained model and fine-tunes it over a single afternoon on ten thousand examples of properly formatted customer support replies, spending a tiny fraction of the original pretraining cost, and ends up with a model that replies in their exact support voice.
The company never touched pretraining directly, they benefited entirely from work someone else already paid for, and simply redirected that existing capability toward their specific need.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming fine-tuning and pretraining require similar amounts of compute, when the gap is typically several orders of magnitude
Expecting fine-tuning to fix a fundamental capability gap that only a stronger pretrained base model can close
Confusing continued pretraining, still using broad general data, with fine-tuning, which uses narrow task specific data
Underestimating how much of the final model quality actually comes from the choice of pretrained base

blocks.text: Practice

Look up the parameter count and, if published, the training data size of a base model you are considering. Compare that figure against the size of a fine-tuning dataset you might realistically collect, and notice just how much smaller the fine-tuning stage really is.
Key Takeaway

Pretraining is a rare, enormous, broadly scoped training run that builds a model general capability, while fine-tuning is a common, small, narrowly scoped training run that redirects an already pretrained model toward a specific task or behavior.
